transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. Before we dive in, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I’ve been catching myself thinking it might be easier if I just didn’t wake up. And sometimes driving home, I wonder if my family or my students would be better off without me. It scares me—I don’t want to do anything about it, but the thoughts are there.
Can you tell me how long you've been experiencing these low moods and thoughts of not wanting to wake up?
About a year and seven months, I think. It started when I took on the STEM assessment redesign along with my regular teaching load.
Have you ever had a period, lasting several days or more, where you felt unusually energetic, elated, or needed much less sleep than usual?
No, I don’t think so. I haven’t noticed any periods like that.

Before this began about a year and seven months ago, have you ever had a distinct period in your life—lasting weeks or more—where you felt similarly depressed, and then it fully lifted before this current episode started?
I’m not really sure. I can’t think of a time before this where I had a stretch like that and then it completely went away.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you also noticed changes in your sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, or feelings of guilt or worthlessness alongside the low mood?

Yes—my sleep has been pretty bad. I’ll be exhausted but still lie awake going over assessment deadlines or things I think I did wrong in class. Then I wake up around four in the morning and usually can’t really get back to sleep.
During this year and seven months, has your low mood been present most days, or have there been stretches of two months or longer where you felt essentially back to your normal self?

It’s been there most days, really. It started about a year and seven months ago, when I took on the STEM assessment redesign alongside my normal teaching load, and I haven’t had a stretch where I felt back to myself for two months or anything like that.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, like teaching or hobbies?

Yeah. I used to look forward to softball, book club, working in my garden, and helping with robotics club. Now I mostly just go through the motions, or cancel, because none of it really feels enjoyable anymore.
Over the past couple of weeks, have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight, either eating much more or much less than usual?
Yeah. On most school days I either forget to eat or just put it off until late afternoon. My clothes have gotten noticeably looser over the past year, and I’m not trying to lose weight.

Over the past couple of weeks, how much have these symptoms interfered with your ability to function at work or in your daily responsibilities—are you still managing to get things done, or has it become very difficult to keep up?

It’s become pretty difficult to keep up. I’m behind on grading and lesson planning, and it’s affecting my classroom. I made a grading mistake recently that really scared me, because I used to be meticulous about that stuff. And outside of work, I’m not showing up for friends or family like I used to. Mostly I just get through the school day and go home exhausted.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports a single, continuous depressive episode lasting ~19 months (no prior distinct episode with full remission, ruling out recurrent depressive disorder F33.2, and no history of manic/hypomanic episodes ruling out bipolar disorder). Core symptoms include depressed mood most days, marked anhedonia (loss of interest in softball, book club, gardening, robotics club), significant unintentional weight loss/appetite disturbance, early morning awakening insomnia, fatigue, feelings of guilt/rumination, impaired concentration, and passive suicidal ideation (thoughts of not waking up, family being 'better off' without him) without active intent or plan. Functional impairment is severe—behind on grading/lesson planning, a significant work error, and social withdrawal from friends/family. The severity, number of symptoms (>5 SIGECAPS criteria), degree of functional impairment, and presence of suicidal ideation without psychotic features support a diagnosis of a single severe depressive episode without psychotic features (F32.2) rather than dysthymia (F34.1, which is milder and chronic) or recurrent depression (F33.2, which requires a prior distinct episode).
